value.overview: The Volcano Junco (Junco vulcani) is a small, high-elevation New World sparrow restricted to the Talamancan mountain region of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is strongly associated with páramo, alpine grassland, low brush, and other open habitats near or above the timberline. The species often forages on the ground and is one of the characteristic birds of the highest mountains in Costa Rica, including Cerro de la Muerte, Cerro Chirripó, and Irazú Volcano.
value.classification: The Volcano Junco belongs to the family Passerellidae, the New World sparrows, and the genus Junco. It is generally treated as a monotypic species.
value.identification: This junco is about 16 cm long, with brown upperparts marked by dark streaking, gray underparts, and dark wings and tail. The head is mostly gray, with a black mask through the eye, a yellow iris, and a pale pink bill. The legs are pinkish. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked than adults. It is usually seen walking or hopping on open ground, often near short shrubs, rocks, or patches of grass.
value.rangeHabitat: The Volcano Junco is endemic to the Talamancan montane region of Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly on the highest peaks and páramo habitats of the Cordillera de Talamanca and other suitable high mountains, including areas around Cerro de la Muerte, Cerro Chirripó, and Irazú Volcano. It typically occupies open grassy slopes, alpine páramo, elfin scrub, and stunted vegetation above about 3,000 meters, although it can occur lower locally where forest has been cleared or suitable habitat is available.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered largely resident in Costa Rica and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Individuals may make local movements along mountain slopes or shift elevations seasonally in response to weather and food availability.
value.breeding: The nest is a lined cup placed on or close to the ground, commonly beneath a log, rock, bush, or overhanging bank of vegetation. Breeding has been associated with the high-elevation wet season, although the timing can vary with local conditions. The clutch generally contains two pale bluish eggs marked with brown. The species’ ground-nesting habit makes nests difficult to detect and potentially vulnerable to trampling in heavily visited alpine areas.
value.dietFeeding: The Volcano Junco feeds mainly on the ground. Its diet includes seeds, fallen berries and other small fruits, insects, and spiders. It searches among short grass, leaf litter, rocks, and low vegetation, usually moving by running and hopping. Small invertebrates are especially useful during breeding, when adults need protein-rich food for developing young.
value.behavior: This species is generally encountered alone, in pairs, or in small groups. It spends much of its time walking and hopping across open ground and usually flies only short distances between feeding sites or patches of cover. Its calls include thin, high notes and clearer whistles, while the song is a varied mixture of squeaks, buzzes, and short musical phrases. It is often approachable in remote high-elevation habitats but may be affected by human activity near popular summits.

conservation.populationTrend: A reliable current population trend is not well documented.
